JSON: Name: probabilistic_anomaly_corpus Title: Anomaly detection with probabilistic sequence models for automatic detection of part-of-speech tagging errors in annotated corpora Short Hypothesis: A sparse Markov transducer–based anomaly detector that ranks tokens by log-likelihood drop when moved from a majority model to an anomalous model will achieve higher precision at fixed recall for detecting POS tagging errors in a manually annotated corpus than a naive Bayes–based anomaly detector. Related Work: Prior work approximates tagging distributions using sequence models (n-grams, HMMs, maximum-entropy, transformation-based taggers) and applies post-hoc cleaning or boosting to improve tagger training data. Anomaly and outlier detection literature uses mixture models and likelihood-based tests to identify elements not generated by the majority distribution; intrusion-detection work applies similar ideas to temporal sequences. Prior probabilistic transducer approaches model conditional mappings from input sequences to outputs but require dense context selection or fixed-order conditioning. Existing corpus-cleaning approaches either (1) rely on manual multi-pass adjudication which is costly, (2) use simple local heuristics that fail in sparse/ambiguous contexts, or (3) apply global models that do not produce ranked, human-verifiable candidate lists. Limitations include sensitivity to the chosen probabilistic model, low power in infrequent or highly ambiguous contexts, poor handling of consistent inter-annotator style differences (which manifest as systematic modes rather than isolated outliers), and lack of quantitative comparisons between sequence-aware anomaly detectors and simpler baselines. Abstract: We address automatic detection of annotation errors in part-of-speech (POS)–tagged corpora by framing corpus cleaning as a probabilistic anomaly-detection problem. The approach fits a generative model over token–context–tag tuples and evaluates each tuple by the change in log likelihood when treated as generated by an anomalous distribution instead of the majority distribution; anomalies are ranked by that score and presented for verification or automatic correction. We instantiate the pipeline with two probability estimators — a sparse Markov transducer that conditions on varying combinations of word and neighboring tags, and a naive Bayes model that assumes conditional independence — and compare their ranked outputs. The main contribution is a reproducible pipeline that (a) produces a compact, prioritized set of candidate annotation errors, (b) quantifies detector behavior under different model choices and priors, and (c) measures the fraction of true annotation errors recoverable by automatic suggested corrections. Expected outcomes include a measurable reduction in human review effort via high-precision candidate lists and an empirical characterization of trade-offs between model complexity and error-detection performance. Experiments: Datasets: primary: tagged portion of the Penn Treebank (~1.25M tokens). Secondary (optional for generalization): at least one additional manually tagged corpus of comparable size. Baselines: (1) naive Bayes anomaly detector conditioned on (word, previous tag, next tag); (2) frequency-based heuristic ranking (lowest conditional tag probability P(tag|word)); (3) random sampling. Proposed models: (A) sparse Markov transducer (SMT) using weighted mixture of context patterns {Wt, Tt-1, Tt+1, WtTt-1, WtTt+1, Tt-1Tt+1, WtTt-1Tt+1} with pseudo-count priors; (B) naive Bayes. Scoring: for each token compute log-likelihood LL_full under the majority model and LL_removed under the model with the token assigned to the anomalous distribution; anomaly score = LL_full - LL_removed (equation-based). Ranking and sampling: sort tokens by score descending; evaluate precision@k for k={100,500,1000,2000,4000}. Human verification: for each k-tier, randomly sample 100 tokens for manual adjudication; label outcomes as true error / unsure / system error. Metrics: precision@k, recall at fixed human-review budget, precision-recall curve, AUC-PR, correction accuracy (fraction of true errors where suggested replacement tag matches adjudicated correct tag), and mean suggested-tag confidence. Experimental setup: train models on full dataset; hold out no extra data for detection (anomaly detection is unsupervised); vary anomaly prior A in {0.001,0.005,0.01,0.02}; perform ablation studies: (i) remove word feature (use only neighboring tags), (ii) remove context tags (use only word), (iii) remove pseudo-count smoothing, (iv) compare fixed-order Markov (trigram) vs SMT. Statistical comparisons: report paired bootstrap confidence intervals for precision@1000 between SMT and naive Bayes; report significance at p<0.05. Repeat human verification with two independent annotators for 10% of samples to estimate inter-annotator agreement. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: model misspecification can cause high false positive rates when the majority distribution is poorly estimated; sparse contexts and rare words yield unreliable likelihood estimates; extreme smoothing or poor prior A choices can mask true anomalies. Data/evaluation biases: evaluation via sampled human adjudication can overestimate performance if samples are drawn from high-score regions only; adjudicator disagreement on boundary cases (tag ambiguity) will limit measurable precision. Scalability and compute: SMT estimation with large context sets and many pseudo-count patterns can be memory- and compute-intensive on multi-million-token corpora; recomputing models after removing detected anomalies may be costly at scale. Generalization limits: approach assumes annotation errors are isolated outliers under a mixture model and will not detect systematic annotator style differences or consistent errors that form a secondary mode; performance may degrade on languages or tagsets with higher ambiguity or on corpora with dense annotation schemas beyond POS tagging.
